s13.quote: Of Cadmus and Amphion. No man’s life
s13.note: The Messenger addresses the elders as neighbours of two founding houses: Cadmus who sowed the city and Amphion who walled it. Both houses ended badly, Amphion's with Niobe's children, whom Antigone took as her own emblem in [[s9]]. The address is a small history of Theban ruin before a new chapter of it is read out.

s13.quote: As of one tenor would I praise or blame,
s13.note: This is the old maxim that no life can be judged while it is still running, here spoken by a servant. Notice that he refuses blame as well as praise. He is about to report a catastrophe caused by his master, and his first move is to decline the role of judge; the judging will be left to the Chorus and, in the end, to Creon himself.

s13.quote: For Fortune with a constant ebb and rise
s13.note: Storr gives a tide; the Greek gives a pair of scales and a building. τύχη (_tyche_, "chance, fortune") is named twice in l. 1158: it ὀρθοῖ (_orthoi_, "sets upright") and it καταρρέπει (_katarrhepei_, "makes the pan sink"). The first verb belongs to Creon's own vocabulary. In [[s3]] he said the gods had set the city upright again and that he would keep it sailing straight. The Messenger now hands that work to luck.

s13.quote: And none can read a mortal’s horoscope.
s13.note: There is no horoscope in Sophocles. The word is μάντις (_mantis_, "prophet, seer", l. 1160): no one is a prophet of what is settled for mortals. This is said a few minutes after Teiresias left the stage having prophesied exactly this. The word comes back twice more in the next sixty lines, and each time it corrects the Messenger.

s13.quote: Was enviable. He had saved this land
s13.note: ζηλωτός (_zelotos_, "enviable", l. 1161) and then σώσας (_sosas_, "having saved") the land from ἐχθρῶν (_echthron_, "enemies", l. 1162). An ordinary Theban grants Creon the whole of his own case: there was a war, there were enemies, he saved the city. I think this matters for how we judge the edict. The play does not want us to think the sorting of friend from enemy was a tyrant's fantasy; it was true, and it was not enough.

s13.quote: A monarch’s powers and ruled the state supreme,
s13.note: _pantele monarchian_ ("complete sole rule", l. 1163), and the verb for his ruling is _euthyne_ ("he steered straight", l. 1164): the ship of state once more. Haemon told him in [[s7]] that a city belonging to one man is no city, and that he would rule a desert well. The Messenger's summary of the good days already contains the fault.

s13.quote: Now all is gone and wasted, for a life
s13.note: The test the Messenger applies is _hedonas_ ("pleasures", l. 1165): when a man has lost those, he is not alive. A tutor should ask whether that is a servant's shallow philosophy or the play's. I think it is closer to the play than it looks. Creon warned his son not to lose his wits for pleasure in a woman, and treated every tie of affection as something a ruler could afford to cut. The Messenger says that what he cut was the life.

s13.quote: Without life’s joys I count a living death.
s13.note: ἔμψυχον (_empsychon_, "with breath in it") and νεκρόν (_nekron_, "corpse"), both in l. 1167: a breathing corpse. The play's central image changes owners here. Antigone was to be the living dead, shut in rock; Teiresias charged Creon with lodging a living soul in a grave. It is Creon who ends that way, in a palace, and he will say so himself at the end.

s13.quote: The pomp and circumstance of kings; but if
s13.note: Storr borrows Othello's phrase. The Greek is plainer and sharper: live with a _tyrannon_ (l. 1169) bearing, a tyrant's outward show. The word need not be abusive in tragedy, but Antigone used the same root in [[s5]] when she said that tyranny is lucky because it can do and say what it likes. Here the show is all that is left of it.

s13.quote: The shadow of a shade, nor would I weigh
s13.note: καπνοῦ σκιᾶς (_kapnou skias_, "the shadow of smoke", l. 1170), and the verb is πριαίμην (_priaimen_, "I would buy", l. 1171): I would not buy the rest from a man at the price of smoke's shadow. Storr's 'weigh' and 'dram' keep a little of the market. It is worth keeping all of it, because Creon has spent the play accusing everyone of being bought. His own goods are now priced at nothing by one of his servants.

s13.quote: What fresh woes bring’st thou to the royal house?
s13.note: _achthos basileon_ ("a burden of the kings", l. 1172). The elders have just finished dancing a hymn in [[s12]] that begged Dionysus to come with healing foot. The next person to arrive is this man. Sophocles likes to place a hopeful song directly before the blow, and the little word for 'again' in the Chorus's question shows they know the pattern too.

s13.quote: Both dead, and they who live deserve to die.
s13.note: The Greek begins with one word, τεθνᾶσιν (_tethnasin_, "they are dead", l. 1173), with no subject at all; 'Both' is Storr's help. And the second half is mistranslated in a way that matters. αἴτιοι θανεῖν (_aitioi thanein_) means the living are responsible for the dying, not that they deserve death. It is the first appearance of the vocabulary of cause and blame that Creon will take on himself at l. 1318.

s13.quote: Haemon; his blood shed by no stranger hand.
s13.note: Αἵμων (_Haimon_) and αἱμάσσεται (_haimassetai_, "is bloodied") sit in the same line (l. 1175): his name is the word for blood, and Sophocles waits until now to use it. The other word is αὐτόχειρ (_autocheir_), which can mean by his own hand or by the hand of his own kin. In this family the two meanings are never far apart, and the Chorus hears both.

s13.quote: What mean ye? by his father’s or his own?
s13.note: _patroias_ ("a father's") or _oikeias_ ("his own", l. 1176). The question is forced by the ambiguity of _autocheir_, but look at what it shows about the elders. Men who have deferred to Creon all day find it perfectly possible that he has killed his son. And the honest answer to their either-or is: both.

s13.quote: His own; in anger for his father’s crime.
s13.note: Two strong words are softened here. μηνίσας (_menisas_, l. 1177) is from the word for the wrath of Achilles and of gods, a lasting rage and not a fit of temper. And φόνου (_phonou_) is 'murder', not 'crime'. The Messenger, who a moment ago would neither praise nor blame, calls the death of Antigone a killing and names its owner.

s13.quote: O prophet, what thou spakest comes to pass.
s13.note: ὦ μάντι (_o manti_, l. 1178): the Chorus speaks to Teiresias, who is not there. Fifty lines after the Messenger said there is no prophet of human affairs, the elders answer that there was one and he was right. ὀρθὸν (_orthon_, "straight, true") is their word for his prophecy. Straightness has passed from the king's steering to the seer's speech.

s13.quote: So stands the case; now ’tis for you to act.
s13.note: Not 'act' but βουλεύειν (_bouleuein_, "to take counsel, deliberate", l. 1179). This begins the run of counsel-words that carries the whole exodos: the Messenger's moral at l. 1242, then Creon's own two words for it in his first lament. The Chorus is being asked for the one thing Thebes has lacked all day, and it will again have very little to offer.

s13.quote: Creon’s unhappy wife, Eurydice.
s13.note: This is the first time the play mentions that Creon has a wife, with fewer than two hundred lines to go. She is _damarta_ ("wedded wife", l. 1181), introduced only to be destroyed. She speaks nine lines. With three actors the part must be doubled, so the voice behind her mask is one we have already heard in another role, though which one cannot be proved.

s13.quote: Comes she by chance or learning her son’s fate?
s13.note: _tychei_ ("by chance", l. 1182): the Messenger's word, taken up at once. The exodos keeps offering chance as an explanation and then withdrawing it. She comes out because she heard, and she heard because she was at the door on her way to pray.

s13.quote: Ye men of Thebes, I overheard your talk.
s13.note: _o pantes astoi_ ("all you townsmen", l. 1183). A queen addresses the citizens in the open, in a play where Creon ruled that women were to be kept indoors and not let range. She has the same instinct as Antigone to speak to the city directly. Unlike Antigone she asks only to be told something.

s13.quote: To Pallas, and was drawing back the bar
s13.note: She was going to _Pallados theas_ ("the goddess Pallas", l. 1184) with prayers. Sophocles stops her with her hand on the bolt, between the house and the city, which is where the whole play has been fought. Her prayer is never made. By the end the Chorus will tell her husband not to pray at all.

s13.quote: There broke a wail that told of household woe
s13.note: οἰκείου κακοῦ (_oikeiou kakou_, "an evil of my own house", l. 1187). The adjective _oikeios_, 'belonging to the house, one's own', is the quiet keyword of this section: the own hand at l. 1176, the native earth of the mound at l. 1203, the private grief at l. 1249. Creon's politics put the house under the city. The exodos is the house's reply.

s13.quote: To one not unacquaint with misery.
s13.note: κακῶν γὰρ οὐκ ἄπειρος (_kakon gar ouk apeiros_, "not without experience of evils", l. 1191). It is her only self-description, and it implies a history the play has not told us: she has lost a son already. The Second Messenger fills this in after she is dead. Keep the phrase in your ear, because the Messenger will reuse its shape when he guesses wrongly about her at l. 1250.

s13.quote: Dear mistress, I was there and will relate
s13.note: _phile despoina_ ("dear mistress", l. 1192), and _paron_ ("being present"): an eyewitness and a servant who uses the language of affection. Why does Sophocles have the catastrophe told to her and not simply to the Chorus? Because this narrative is itself an action. We watch it land on a listener, and by its last line it has killed her.

s13.quote: Liars hereafter? Truth is ever best.
s13.note: _orthon_ (l. 1195) again: truth is always the straight thing. He refuses to soften anything, and he keeps his word, down to the spitting. I would not take the maxim as the play's. A mother is told in exact detail how her son died cursing his father, and she walks inside and kills herself. Straightness, in speech as in government, has a cost that the straight speaker does not pay.

s13.quote: The corse of Polyneices, gnawn and mauled,
s13.note: _kynosparakton_ ("torn by dogs", l. 1198), lying _nelees_ ("unpitied", l. 1197). So Antigone's dust and libations did not protect the body. Whatever her two visits achieved in the eyes of the gods, the edict was carried out to the letter on the flesh, exactly as Creon first announced it in [[s3]].

s13.quote: Was lying yet. We offered first a prayer
s13.note: 'First' is the crux. In [[s11]] the Chorus told Creon to free the girl and then bury the dead; he does it the other way round. Some call this a dramatic convenience, since Antigone has to be dead. I think it is characteristic. Teiresias's charge was about the corpse, the altars and the city's pollution, and Creon repairs the public, ritual damage before the private one. He is still putting the city first, and it costs him the three lives.

s13.quote: To Pluto and the goddess of cross-ways,
s13.note: ἐνοδίαν θεὸν (_enodian theon_, "the goddess of the roads", l. 1199) is Hecate. They ask the powers below to hold their ὀργὰς εὐμενεῖς (_orgas eumeneis_, "angers kindly", l. 1200). _Orge_ has been Creon's own failing all day; now it is the gods who have it and he who must placate. Storr's 'contrite hearts' is his invention. The Greek reports a rite correctly performed and says nothing about anyone's heart.

s13.quote: Then laved with lustral waves the mangled corse,
s13.note: _lousantes hagnon loutron_ ("washing him with pure washing", l. 1201). In [[s9]] Antigone said she had washed and dressed her dead with her own hands. This one she could only sprinkle with dust. The king's party now does for Polyneices the full version of the act for which she was condemned, and the Messenger reports it without a flicker.

s13.quote: And to his memory piled a mighty mound
s13.note: τύμβον ὀρθόκρανον οἰκείας χθονὸς (_tymbon orthokranon oikeias chthonos_, "a high-headed mound of his own native earth", l. 1203). Storr's 'mother earth' loses the point that it is Theban soil, the land Polyneices came to burn, now called his own. And there is _orthos_ again inside the adjective: the one thing Creon sets upright today is the traitor's tomb. It is done properly and it takes time, and the time is spent while Antigone is alone in the cave.

s13.quote: The bridal chamber of the maid and Death,
s13.note: νυμφεῖον Ἅιδου (_nympheion Haidou_, "bridal chamber of Hades", l. 1205). This was Antigone's own cry in [[s9]], 'O tomb, O bridal chamber'. Her metaphor has become the ordinary way a palace servant refers to the place. The play has a habit of making her figures of speech come true, and this is the last and worst instance.

s13.quote: Heard from that godless shrine a far shrill wail,
s13.note: Neither 'godless' nor 'shrine' is right. The phrase is ἀκτέριστον ἀμφὶ παστάδα (_akteriston amphi pastada_, l. 1207): around the bride-room that has had no funeral rites. _Akteristos_ is the word Teiresias used of Polyneices' corpse. The condition of being unburied has not been cured by the mound; it has moved across the plain to her.

s13.quote: Am I a prophet? miserable me!
s13.note: μάντις (_mantis_, l. 1212), the third time in the exodos. The man who told Teiresias that the whole tribe of prophets loves money now finds he can foretell things himself. All it takes is knowing what you have done. It is the only moment of foresight Creon has in the play, and it comes a few yards from the tomb.

s13.quote: Is this the saddest path I ever trod?
s13.note: Roads run through the end of the play. Here it is the most unfortunate path of all he has walked; at l. 1274 the god drives him into wild roads; in his last words every way is aslant. The superlative is built on _tyche_, so even at this moment the report is using the Messenger's word for luck.

s13.quote: ’Tis my son’s voice that calls me. On press on,
s13.note: σαίνει (_sainei_, l. 1214) is a strange verb to find here. Its ordinary sense is what a dog does when it fawns on its master, and so it comes to mean a sound that greets or touches you. Storr's 'calls' is too clean. The voice reaches Creon like a caress from something he knows, a few lines after we heard what dogs had done to the other body.

s13.quote: Where rocks down-torn have made a gap, look in
s13.note: _lithospade_ ("where stones have been dragged away", l. 1216): someone has already broken in. Haemon left the stage at the end of [[s7]] and has had the whole length of two odes and the Teiresias scene to get here. Note also that Creon sends his servants to look. Even now, he gives the order and others go first.

s13.quote: The voice of Haemon or am heaven-deceived.
s13.note: _theoisi kleptomai_ ("I am cheated by the gods", l. 1218), literally robbed by them. In [[s3]] Creon knew exactly what the gods would and would not do, and mocked the idea that they cared for the corpse. Now he allows that they might be tricking his ears. His confidence about the divine has gone before he has seen anything.

s13.quote: We looked, and in the craven’s vaulted gloom
s13.note: 'Craven's' in this text is a misprint for 'cavern's'. The Greek is _loisthioi tymbeumati_ ("the furthest part of the tomb", l. 1220). She has gone as far in as the place allows. Sophocles gives her no last words and no narrated death; she is simply found, at the back of what Creon built.

s13.quote: I saw the maiden lying strangled there,
s13.note: She is not lying. κρεμαστὴν αὐχένος (_kremasten auchenos_, "hanging by the neck", l. 1221) is what they see. Creon had her walled up with food so that the city would have no blood on its hands and the choice between living and dying would be hers. She made it at once. The scheme to keep himself clean failed because she would not wait to be pardoned.

s13.quote: A noose of linen twined about her neck;
s13.note: _brochoi mitodei sindonos_ ("a threaded noose of fine linen", l. 1222). A _sindon_ is good cloth, very likely something she was wearing, perhaps her veil. Ismene described their mother's death in [[s1]] in nearly the same terms, a twisted noose. Antigone ends as Jocasta did, and the bridal chamber gets its bride hanged in her own finery.

s13.quote: Death-wedded, and his father’s cruelty.
s13.note: πατρὸς ἔργα (_patros erga_, "his father's deeds", l. 1225). 'Cruelty' is Storr's interpretation; Haemon laments what his father has done. Hold on to the plain word _ergon_, because three lines later Creon uses it of Haemon.

s13.quote: What hast thou done? What ailed thee? What mischance
s13.note: οἷον ἔργον (_hoion ergon_, "what a deed", l. 1228), and then: what νοῦν (_noun_, "mind") did you have, how were you διεφθάρης (_diephthares_, "ruined", l. 1229)? Creon's first words to his son are still an inquiry into the son's wits. That was his line throughout [[s7]], that the boy's judgment had been corrupted by a woman. He has come to undo his decree and has not yet stopped diagnosing other people.

s13.quote: Come forth, my son; thy father supplicates.
s13.note: _hikesios se lissomai_ ("as a suppliant I beg you", l. 1230). The king who told his son that a father's will must be obeyed in everything is now in the posture of the weakest person in Greek society. A suppliant has a claim the gods protect. Haemon refuses it, and that refusal is part of what he turns his anger on a moment later.

s13.quote: But the son glared at him with tiger eyes,
s13.note: There is no tiger: _agriois ossoisi_ ("with wild eyes", l. 1231). The adjective returns when Creon says the god drove him into wild roads. Haemon's last words in [[s7]] were that his father would never set eyes on his face again. He was wrong by one look, and this is the look.

s13.quote: Spat in his face, and then, without a word,
s13.note: πτύσας προσώπῳ (_ptysas prosopoi_, l. 1232) may be literal, as Storr takes it, or may mean loathing shown in his own face; commentators divide. Either way the participle is one we have heard. In [[s7]] Creon told Haemon to treat the girl as an enemy and let her go, πτύσας (_ptysas_, "spitting her out", l. 653). The son gives the word back. And κοὐδὲν ἀντειπών (_kouden anteipon_, "answering nothing"): the young man who argued so patiently has finished with argument.

s13.quote: Drew his two-hilted sword and smote, but missed
s13.note: _diplous knodontas_ (l. 1233) are the two prongs of the cross-guard, so he draws it to the hilt. This is attempted parricide in the family of Oedipus. Aristotle cites Haemon and Creon in the Poetics as his example of the weakest plot pattern, where someone knowingly sets out to do the deed and then does not: it is repellent and nothing comes of it. He adds that it is rarely used, and here it is only narrated.

s13.quote: Wroth with himself, poor wretch, incontinent
s13.note: _hautoi cholotheis_ ("enraged at himself", l. 1235). 'Incontinent' means immediately, with no pause, which renders the Greek 'just as he was'. And 'wroth with himself' is exact: he has just tried to kill his father and failed. The suicide is partly love and partly horror at what he nearly did, and it is the anger of l. 1177 turned round.

s13.quote: Home, but yet breathing clasped in his lax arms
s13.note: The word is not 'breathing' but ἔμφρων (_emphron_, "in his right mind, conscious", l. 1237). It belongs to the _phronein_ family the play has fought over, and the Messenger gives it to the dying boy, a few lines after Creon asked what had become of his mind. The verb for the embrace, προσπτύσσεται (_prosptyssetai_), sounds like the spitting of l. 1232 though it is a different root. The two gestures, at father and at bride, are made to chime.

s13.quote: The maid, her pallid cheek incarnadined
s13.note: _leukei pareiai phoiniou stalagmatos_ ("on her white cheek, of red drops", l. 1239). Storr reaches for Macbeth's word for staining red. White and red are a bride's colours, and many readers take the spurt of blood as the consummation the two were denied. It is the only wedding either of them gets, and the Messenger says so in the next lines.

s13.quote: Two corpses, one in death. His marriage rites
s13.note: νεκρὸς περὶ νεκρῷ (_nekros peri nekroi_, "corpse around corpse", l. 1240), and the rites are νυμφικὰ (_nymphika_, "bridal") τέλη (_tele_, l. 1241), a word that means both rites and completion. In [[s7]] Creon said the girl could find a husband in the house of Hades. She has, and it is his son. The motif of the bride of Death, which was hers throughout, is completed with the bridegroom as the one who marries into death.

s13.quote: Mortals’ unwisdom is the worst of all.
s13.note: τὴν ἀβουλίαν (_ten aboulian_, "lack of counsel, ill counsel", l. 1242) is narrower than 'unwisdom'. It answers an exchange in [[s11]]: Teiresias asked how far good counsel, εὐβουλία (_euboulia_, l. 1050), is the best of possessions, and Creon replied that not thinking is the worst of harms. Grammatically it is Haemon who has 'shown' this. Whose bad counsel he showed is left unsaid, in front of the wife of the man it points to.

s13.quote: Without a word importing good or ill.
s13.note: She is _phroude_ ("gone", l. 1245), and the Chorus calls her simply _he gyne_ ("the woman", l. 1244). The silent exit of a woman who has just understood everything is a device Sophocles uses for Jocasta and for Deianeira too. It comes straight after Haemon's 'answering nothing'. In this exodos the people who stop speaking are the ones about to act.

s13.quote: I marvel too, but entertain good hope.
s13.note: _elpisin de boskomai_ ("I feed on hopes", l. 1246): the verb is used of grazing animals. In [[s6]] the Chorus sang that wide-wandering hope helps many men and cheats many others. The Messenger who opened by saying nothing can be predicted now predicts, on the strength of what he would like to be true.

s13.quote: Would with her maidens mourn a private loss.
s13.note: He hopes she will not wail ἐς πόλιν (_es polin_, "before the city", l. 1247) but keep it a πένθος οἰκεῖον (_penthos oikeion_, "a grief of the house", l. 1249). It is Creon's division of the world, repeated by a decent man as plain good manners: grief belongs indoors, with the women. Antigone's offence was to carry a house's mourning out into the city. Eurydice takes hers back in, and it is no safer there.

s13.quote: Trust me, she is discreet and will not err.
s13.note: γνώμης γὰρ οὐκ ἄπειρος (_gnomes gar ouk apeiros_, "not without experience of judgment", l. 1250) copies the shape of her own phrase at l. 1191, experience of evils. The Messenger swaps the noun and gets her wrong. ἁμαρτάνειν (_hamartanein_, "to go wrong, to miss") is the verb, and within ten lines the Chorus will use it of Creon. The speaker has misplaced who in this house is liable to error.

s13.quote: Is no less ominous than excessive grief.
s13.note: ἄγαν σιγὴ βαρὺ (_agan sige bary_, "too much silence is a heavy thing", l. 1251). It is the Greek rule of nothing in excess, applied for once to quiet. The elders finally read a situation correctly and in time, and it is still too late to matter. The weight in _bary_ returns when Creon says the god struck his head with a great weight.

s13.quote: Some fell design. It may be thou art right:
s13.note: He fears something _katascheton_ ("held down", l. 1253) hidden in a _kardiai thymoumenei_ ("a heart in passion", l. 1254). Then he goes into the house. That clears the stage for Creon and puts a witness indoors. The Second Messenger who comes out at l. 1278 is called in Greek the one who brings news from within, and it is natural to play him as this same man.

s13.quote: Evidence he with him bears
s13.note: He carries, _dia cheiros_ ("in his hands", l. 1258), something _episemon_ ("clearly marked"): a memorial. Storr makes it legal evidence, but the Greek noun is the word for a monument to the dead. Creon enters with Haemon's body in his arms or with his hand on the bier. He left the stage at the end of [[s11]] giving orders about axes; this is what he brings back.

s13.quote: ’Gainst a king such charge to make
s13.note: _ei themis eipein_ ("if it is lawful to say so", l. 1259). With the dead son in front of them the elders still ask leave to speak. It is the truest thing in the portrait of this Chorus: they have known for some time, and they say it only when the king can no longer hurt them.

s13.quote: The guilt is his and his alone.
s13.note: Two of the play's great words are flattened into 'guilt'. The ruin is not ἀλλοτρίαν (_allotrian_, "someone else's", l. 1259) ἄτην (_aten_, "ruin, delusion", l. 1260); he himself was ἁμαρτών (_hamarton_, "the one who erred"). In [[s6]] the Chorus sang of _ate_ as what a god sends on a house, generation after generation. Here they say this _ate_ came from nowhere outside. It is their one firm verdict, and it will not sit easily with what they tell him about fate at l. 1337.

s13.quote: Woe for sin of minds perverse,
s13.note: φρενῶν δυσφρόνων ἁμαρτήματα (_phrenon dysphronon hamartemata_, "errors of ill-thinking thoughts", l. 1261a). 'Sin' brings in a Christian idea; these are mistakes, misses. The root for mind is doubled, a mind that minded badly, and he calls the errors στερεὰ (_sterea_, "hard, stubborn", l. 1262). Hardness was his charge against Antigone in [[s5]], where he said the stiffest iron snaps soonest. He is now singing, too, for the first time in the play.

s13.quote: Behold us slain and slayers, all akin.
s13.note: ἐμφυλίους (_emphylious_, "of one stock", l. 1264): killers and killed within one family. It is the word for bloodshed among one's own, and it takes the play back to its first fact, two brothers dead by each other's hands on one day. Creon legislated about that pair as if he stood outside it. He is addressing the Chorus, who are told to look, and he includes himself in what they see.

s13.quote: Woe for my counsel dire, conceived in sin.
s13.note: ἄνολβα βουλευμάτων (_anolba bouleumaton_, "the unblessedness of my counsels", l. 1265). Nothing was 'conceived in sin'; Storr's piety is running ahead of the text. The noun is the counsel-word again, and _anolba_ denies the prosperity the Messenger began with. Creon is confirming, term for term, the report that was given in his absence.

s13.quote: The fault was mine, mine only, O my son!
s13.note: δυσβουλίαις (_dysbouliais_, "ill counsels", l. 1269): mine, he says, not yours. That answers his own question at the tomb, where he asked what had gone wrong with Haemon's mind. The same word was Antigone's in [[s1]], when she told Ismene to leave her to her own ill counsel. She used it with scorn for the cautious; he uses it as a confession. I think the play means the two uses to be weighed against each other.

s13.quote: Too late thou seemest to perceive the truth.
s13.note: Not truth but justice: ὀψὲ τὴν δίκην ἰδεῖν (_opse ten diken idein_, "late to see justice", l. 1270). _Dike_ is what Antigone claimed for herself in [[s5]], the Justice who lives with the gods below. The Chorus concedes it to her without naming her. They might have added that they saw it late themselves.

s13.quote: By sorrow schooled. Heavy the hand of God,
s13.note: ἔχω μαθὼν (_echo mathon_, "I have learned", l. 1272). This is learning through suffering, the pattern Aeschylus made famous, and it prepares the last word of the play. Then at once θεὸς (_theos_, "a god", l. 1273) struck him on the head with a μέγα βάρος (_mega baros_, "great weight"). Is he shifting the blame he took a moment ago? I think not. For a Greek the same act can be wholly a man's error and wholly a god's blow.

s13.quote: Thorny and rough the paths my feet have trod,
s13.note: The god shook him into _agriais hodois_ ("wild ways", l. 1274). It is the adjective the Messenger used of Haemon's eyes. In the ode on man in [[s4]] the wild was what human skill tames; here a ruler is driven out into it.

s13.quote: Humbled my pride, my pleasure turned to pain;
s13.note: There is no pride in the Greek. What is overturned and λακπάτητον (_lakpateton_, "trampled underfoot", l. 1275) is χαράν (_charan_, "joy"). That is the Messenger's criterion come home: without τὸ χαίρειν (_to chairein_, "rejoicing", l. 1170) a man is a breathing corpse. Creon has not heard that speech, and he supplies its key word himself.

s13.quote: Sorrows are thine, my lord, and more to come,
s13.note: _echon te kai kektemenos_ ("as one who both has and owns", l. 1278). It is a phrase for property, used of a man of means, and what Creon has and holds is evils: one lot _pro cheiron_ ("in his hands", l. 1279), another stored in the house. The Messenger's 'ample store of wealth' is audited here, and the phrase also confirms that he is holding the body.

s13.quote: Thy wife, the mother of thy dead son here,
s13.note: παμμήτωρ (_pammetor_, "mother in the fullest sense, all mother", l. 1282) is a rare, heavy compound. She is defined entirely by motherhood, and she dies of it. The plain γυνὴ (_gyne_, "woman, wife") that begins the line is the word Creon has used all day with contempt.

s13.quote: How bottomless the pit!
s13.note: Storr drops both ideas. δυσκάθαρτος Ἅιδου λιμήν (_dyskathartos Haidou limen_, l. 1284a) is the harbour of Hades, hard to cleanse or hard to appease. The ship of state from [[s3]] has reached port, and the port is death. And _katharsis_ is exactly what Creon tried to secure when he chose a death for Antigone that would leave the city unpolluted. The stain cannot now be washed out of his own house.

s13.quote: To slay anew a man already slain?
s13.note: ἐπεξειργάσω (_epexeirgaso_, "you have finished off", l. 1288), with a dead man as its object. Teiresias asked him in [[s11]] what valour there was in killing the dead a second time, with ἐπικτανεῖν (_epiktanein_, "to kill over again", l. 1030). That was Creon's treatment of Polyneices. He now describes his own state in the image that was used to reproach him.

s13.quote: Stroke upon stroke, first son, then mother slain?
s13.note: The Greek calls her death σφάγιον (_sphagion_, "a sacrificial slaughter", l. 1291) and γυναικεῖον (_gynaikeion_, "a woman's", l. 1292). Creon swore more than once that no woman would get the better of him. The last blow he takes is described, by him, as a woman's death lying on top of the ruin. The sacrificial word is literal, as we are about to hear: she died at the altar.

s13.quote: Look for thyself. She lies for all to view.
s13.note: 'She is no longer _en mychois_ ("in the inner rooms", l. 1293)'. The palace doors open and the body is shown, probably wheeled out on the platform the Greek theatre used for interior scenes. The innermost part of the house, the women's part, is turned out into public view. Creon now stands between two corpses.

s13.quote: A minute past I clasped a lifeless son,
s13.note: He has the child _en cheiressin_ ("in his arms", l. 1297) and sees the other body _enanta_ ("opposite", l. 1298). The line describes the stage picture. It is also a picture of his reasoning in [[s7]], where he told his son that a bad wife is a cold thing to hold and other fields could be ploughed.

s13.quote: Beside the altar on a keen-edged sword
s13.note: The line is corrupt in the manuscripts and the sword is partly an editorial repair, but βωμία (_bomia_, "at the altar", l. 1301) is secure. This is the household altar, the Zeus of the courtyard by whom Creon swore in [[s5]] that no closeness of kin would save Antigone. Teiresias reported the city's altars fouled with carrion from the unburied son of Oedipus. The altar of Creon's own house is now fouled with his wife's blood.

s13.quote: She mourned for Megareus who nobly died
s13.note: Μεγαρέως κλεινὸν λάχος (_Megareos kleinon lachos_, "the glorious lot of Megareus", l. 1303); some editors read a word for his empty bed instead. The play does not explain this. In the legend another son of Creon died for the city during the siege, the Menoeceus of Euripides' Phoenician Women, and Eurydice plainly holds her husband to account for that death as well. It is the misery she alluded to on entering.

s13.quote: She cursed thee, the slayer of her child.
s13.note: παιδοκτόνῳ (_paidoktonoi_, "child-killer", l. 1305) is the last word of the report and of her life as we hear it, and ἐφυμνήσασα (_ephymnesasa_, "chanting over you") makes the curse a kind of hymn. He laid a hand on neither son. The word does not care. A house that spent the day pronouncing on the curse of the Labdacids ends with a curse of its own, spoken at its own altar.

s13.quote: O for a two-edged sword to slay outright
s13.note: _amphithektoi xiphei_ ("a sword sharpened on both edges", l. 1308) echoes the _oxythektoi_ ("keen-whetted", l. 1301) blade of his wife. He asks why no one has struck him. Antigone, Haemon and Eurydice each died by their own hand. Creon asks someone else to do it, and no one does. Whether that is cowardice or the harder sentence is a fair question, and I think the play intends the second.

s13.quote: As author of both deaths, hers and her son’s.
s13.note: Storr's 'hers' is almost certainly wrong. The Greek says he was charged with the αἰτίαν (_aitian_, "responsibility", l. 1312) for 'these deaths and those', which on the natural reading means Haemon's and Megareus's. ἐπεσκήπτου (_epeskeptou_, l. 1313) is a word with a legal ring, a formal denunciation. The dead woman has served an indictment, and the man who was judge all day is the accused.

s13.quote: With her own hand she stabbed herself to the heart.
s13.note: _autocheir_ (l. 1315) for the third time in the play's last third, and the blow goes under the _hepar_ ("liver"), the Greek seat of the passions. Antigone hanged herself, the death tragedy usually gives to women; Eurydice uses a blade, as the men do. Nicole Loraux built an argument on that distinction. Here it suggests that the silent wife, not the defiant niece, is the one who dies like a soldier.

s13.quote: I am the guilty cause. I did the deed,
s13.note: The pronoun 'I' is said three times in two lines, with _ekanon_ ("I killed", l. 1319) and _etymon_ ("the truth", l. 1320); and just before, the _aitias_ (l. 1318) can be fitted to no other mortal. Compare the ruler of [[s3]], whose speech was just as full of 'I' in announcing who he was and what he had decided. He still talks about himself. But this is the only full acceptance of responsibility anyone makes in the play, and it is unqualified.

s13.quote: A cipher, less than nothing; no delay!
s13.note: He asks to be taken _ekpodon_ ("out of the way", l. 1321), one who exists no more than _medena_ ("a nobody", l. 1325). A cipher is a zero. In the morning he said that a man is not known until he has held power. By evening he has been known, and this is his own reckoning of the result. It also answers the Messenger's breathing corpse from the inside.

s13.quote: Well said, if in disaster aught is well
s13.note: Storr has dropped the most pointed word in the line. κέρδη παραινεῖς (_kerde paraineis_, "you counsel profit"), if there is any κέρδος (_kerdos_, "profit", l. 1326) among evils. _Kerdos_ was Creon's explanation for everything: the guards were bribed, the prophet was bought. The Chorus hands the word back at the end. The only gain left to him is to be got out of sight quickly.

s13.quote: Come, Fate, a friend at need,
s13.note: There is no friend in the Greek. He calls for the finest of deaths, the one that is ὕπατος (_hypatos_, "supreme", l. 1331) because it brings his last day. Storr's 'friend', twice, fills a real absence: Creon sorted the world into friends and enemies, and by now he has no _philos_ left alive to name. The wish for a fine death is Antigone's from [[s1]], where dying for her brother would be noble. She got hers. He will not get his.

s13.quote: Let me not look upon another day!
s13.note: _amar_ ("day", l. 1332). The Chorus entered in [[s2]] greeting the sunbeam, the fairest light ever to shine on seven-gated Thebes, and the whole action has taken one day since. The elders welcomed that dawn as deliverance. The king they served through it now asks not to see the next one.

s13.quote: This for the morrow; to us are present needs
s13.note: _mellonta tauta_ ("those things are in the future", l. 1334). The Chorus turns to _ton prokeimenon_ ("what lies before us"), a participle from the verb used of a body laid out for burial. I would not press it, but two bodies are lying before them. After all the day's argument about burial, the practical question at the end is once again who will see to the dead.

s13.quote: O pray not, prayers are idle; from the doom
s13.note: _proseuchou_ ("pray", l. 1337) is forbidden, because the disaster is _pepromenes_ ("fated"). The same elders sang a whole ode of prayer in [[s12]], and Eurydice was on her way to pray when the news reached her. How does 'fated' square with 'his own error' at l. 1260? The Chorus does not say. I read it as their meaning that the consequences are now fixed, not that the choices were.

s13.quote: Away with me, a worthless wretch who slew
s13.note: _mataion_ ("futile, foolish, empty", l. 1339), and the noun it qualifies is the word for man in the strong, male sense. Creon's fear throughout [[s5]] and [[s7]] was of not being the man, of being beaten by a woman. His last description of himself keeps the noun and empties it.

s13.quote: Unwitting thee, my son, thy mother too.
s13.note: _ouch hekon_ ("not willingly", l. 1340). After 'I killed you' comes the plea that he did not mean to. Both are true, and Greek thought kept them apart: he is the cause and he had no intent. But 'unwitting' is generous. He was told, by Antigone, Haemon, the citizens through Haemon, and Teiresias. He addresses the two bodies directly, and Antigone is not among those he names.

s13.quote: Whither to turn I know now; every way
s13.note: 'Now' in this text is a misprint for 'not'. Everything in his hands is λέχρια (_lechria_, "aslant, crooked", l. 1345). That is the exact opposite of _orthos_, the upright and straight that he promised the city and that the exodos has been taking from him word by word, giving it to fortune, to the prophet, to the truth, to a tomb. The text is damaged just here, but this word is his last image of his own government.

s13.quote: Of crushing Fate.
s13.note: _potmos dyskomistos_ ("a fate hard to carry", l. 1346) has leapt on his head, as the god's weight did at l. 1273. He is led into the house alive. Left in view are the elders and two bodies, a wife and a son. Antigone's body is not brought back, nobody has spoken her name since the tomb, and Ismene is not thought of. The play named for her ends as the ruin of the man who condemned her, and I think both halves of that fact are intended.

s13.quote: Of happiness the chiefest part
s13.note: τὸ φρονεῖν (_to phronein_, "thinking rightly, good sense", l. 1347) is by far the first part of εὐδαιμονίας (_eudaimonias_, "happiness, flourishing"). This is what the Chorus says the play has taught. The trouble is that everyone claimed it. Creon denied it to Antigone, Haemon and Teiresias in turn, and told the seer that μὴ φρονεῖν (_me phronein_, "not thinking", l. 1051) was the worst harm. The moral names the prize without saying who held it.

s13.quote: And to defraud the gods in aught
s13.note: ἀσεπτεῖν (_aseptein_, "to act impiously", l. 1350) appears only here in the play, and 'defraud' is too commercial for it. It is the negative of the reverence Antigone claimed in her last words in [[s9]], that she suffers for having revered reverence. So the Chorus's rule vindicates her piety. It does so without her name, as a rule about the gods' due, which is how these men have preferred to state everything.

s13.quote: Swelling words of high-flown might
s13.note: μεγάλοι δὲ λόγοι (_megaloi de logoi_, "great words", l. 1350) of the ὑπεραύχων (_hyperauchon_, "the over-boastful", l. 1351). They mean Creon. But in [[s2]] these same men sang that Zeus hates the boasts of a big tongue, meaning the Argive attackers. Their wisdom at the end is the proverb they started with. And Antigone spoke great words too; the Chorus told her so. The maxim is too wide to tell her apart from her judge.

s13.quote: Mightily the gods do smite.
s13.note: The gods are Storr's addition. The Greek says that great words pay back μεγάλας πληγὰς (_megalas plegas_, "great blows", l. 1351), with ἀποτίσαντες (_apotisantes_, "having paid in full", l. 1352). It is a debt and its settlement, the last of the play's money words. The blows echo the fresh πλήγμασιν (_plegmasin_, l. 1283) that killed Eurydice. No agent is named, and the sentence reads more like a law of how things go than a judgment handed down.

s13.quote: Wisdom brings to age at last.
s13.note: γήρᾳ τὸ φρονεῖν ἐδίδαξαν (_gerai to phronein edidaxan_, "they teach good sense in old age", l. 1353); the play's last word is 'taught'. In [[s7]] Creon asked whether men of his years were to be taught sense by a boy, and Haemon said there is no shame in learning. Does the play agree with its Chorus? I think it finds the lines true and far too small. The lesson was bought with three people who will never be old, and the good sense the elders praise is the caution that would have left Polyneices to the dogs.
